mainTopic: What a נדר on a food includes: products made from the fruit, and how plain food words are read by normal usage, place and time.
overview: The amud has two משניות about how far a נדר on a food reaches. In the first, the תנא קמא says a vow on dates or late grapes does not forbid date honey or late-grape vinegar. רבי יהודה בן בתירא says a product called by the fruit's name is forbidden too, and חכמים permit it. The גמרא asks how חכמים differ from the תנא קמא. It answers with a ברייתא of רבי שמעון בן אלעזר: if both the fruit and its product are normally eaten, a vow on one forbids both. If only the product is eaten, the vow forbids only the product. The second משנה teaches that a plain word like wine, oil, honey or vegetables covers only the standard kind, not kinds called by a name with an extra describing word. A ברייתא adds that what 'oil' means depends on the place, and a doubt makes both oils forbidden because ספק איסורא לחומרא. It also teaches that 'vegetables' means garden vegetables in regular years and field vegetables in שביעית. The amud ends as רבי אבהו begins a teaching in the name of רבי חנינא בן גמליאל, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: A vow on dates or late grapes does not forbid their products
steps.stepSummary: The תנא קמא of the משנה rules that a vow on dates still allows date honey, and a vow on late grapes still allows their vinegar.
steps.simpleTranslation: Someone who vowed not to eat dates may still eat date honey. Someone who vowed not to eat late grapes may still use vinegar made from late grapes.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה opens with two cases where a person vows off a fruit. The ruling is that the liquid made from that fruit stays permitted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea is that a vow covers only what the person named. Date honey and grape vinegar are separate products, so a vow on 'dates' or 'late grapes' does not reach them.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה
One who makes a vow
Dates
Date honey, the syrup that comes from dates
Late grapes that ripen at the end of the season
Vinegar

phrases.english: MISHNA:
One who vows off dates
is permitted to eat date honey.
One who vows off late grapes
is permitted to use vinegar of late grapes.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַנּוֹדֵר מִן הַתְּמָרִים מוּתָּר בִּדְבַשׁ תְּמָרִים
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A vow on a fruit (dates, late grapes) does not forbid the liquid that comes from it.

steps.title: A product named after the fruit is included in the vow
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה בן בתירא says that if a product is called by the fruit's name, a vow on the fruit forbids the product too. חכמים permit it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה בן בתירא says: if a food's product is called by the food's name, then someone who vows off the food is also forbidden in what comes out of it. But the חכמים permit it.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה brings an opinion that disagrees with the תנא קמא. It ends with חכמים, who permit the product.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי יהודה בן בתירא, the name matters. 'Date honey' still carries the name 'dates', so a person who vowed off dates had it in mind too. חכמים reject this and permit the product, which sounds just like the תנא קמא.

keyTerms.meaning: The name of its offspring, meaning the product that comes from it
Is called by its name
What comes out of it (its juice or liquid)
The Sages permit it

steps.confusionAlert: The חכמים at the end sound exactly like the תנא קמא at the start. That is not a mistake, and the גמרא is about to ask about it.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira says:
Any food whose product is called by its name,
phrases.notes: Like 'date honey' or 'late-grape vinegar', where the product's name includes the fruit.

phrases.english: and one vows off it,
he is forbidden in what comes out of it.
But the Rabbis permit it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a disputing opinion to the תנא קמא, and then חכמים who permit
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יהודה בן בתירא: a product that carries the fruit's name is included in a vow on the fruit. חכמים: it is permitted.

steps.title: Aren't חכמים the same as the תנא קמא?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the משנה lists חכמים separately, when they seem to say exactly what the תנא קמא said.
steps.simpleTranslation: חכמים are the same as the תנא קמא!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא notices that חכמים and the תנא קמא both permit the product. It asks what difference there could be between them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A משנה does not usually repeat the same view twice under two names. So there must be some case where חכמים and the תנא קמא rule differently, and the גמרא wants to find it.

keyTerms.meaning: The Talmud's discussion of the משנה
That is the same as
The first, unnamed opinion in the משנה

phrases.english: GEMARA:
The Rabbis are the same as the first tanna!
phrases.notes: The word in square brackets is filled in by the corrected text; it tells you who the question is about.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions why the משנה repeats the same view under two names
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What is the practical difference between the תנא קמא and חכמים?

steps.title: The difference is the rule of רבי שמעון בן אלעזר: when both fruit and product are eaten
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the two differ over a ברייתא. Its first rule says that when both the fruit and its product are normally eaten, a vow on either one forbids both.
steps.simpleTranslation: There is a difference between them: the ברייתא that teaches this principle in the name of רבי שמעון בן אלעזר. Anything normally eaten as is, whose product is also normally eaten, like dates and date honey: if someone vows off the fruit, the product is forbidden too. If he vows off the product, the fruit is forbidden too.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the difference between חכמים and the תנא קמא depends on a ברייתא. It begins quoting that ברייתא's first rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא looks at how people really eat. When both the fruit and its product are normal foods, like dates and date honey, people treat them as one food, so a vow on either covers both. This would forbid date honey, unlike the plain ruling of the תנא קמא.

keyTerms.meaning: There is a difference between them
That which was taught in a ברייתא
A general principle
It is normally eaten (in its own form)

phrases.english: There is a difference between them
regarding that which is taught in a baraita:

phrases.aramaic: כְּלָל זֶה אָמַר רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן אֶלְעָזָר:
phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar said this principle:
Anything that is normally eaten as it is,
and what comes out of it is also normally eaten,
for example, dates and date honey:
if he vowed off it, he is forbidden in what comes out of it;
if he vows off what comes out of it, he is forbidden in it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question by pointing to a ברייתא that splits the two views
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The תנא קמא and חכמים differ over רבי שמעון בן אלעזר's rule. Its first part: when both fruit and product are normally eaten, a vow on either forbids both.

steps.title: When only the product is eaten, the vow covers only the product
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא's second rule: if the fruit itself is not normally eaten but its product is, a vow on the fruit forbids only the product, since that is what the person meant.
steps.simpleTranslation: Anything not normally eaten as it is, whose product is normally eaten: if someone vows off it, only the product is forbidden, because he meant only the product.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes quoting the ברייתא of רבי שמעון בן אלעזר. This second rule completes the answer to how חכמים differ from the תנא קמא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A vow follows what the person meant. If nobody eats this fruit as is, like late grapes, his vow must have meant the product, so the vinegar is forbidden and the grapes are permitted. חכמים accept this split; the תנא קמא permits the product in both cases without dividing.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not normally eaten as it is
He intended, he had in mind
Only this is forbidden

steps.whatToRemember: A vow follows how people really eat and what the person meant. If both fruit and product are eaten (dates), a vow on one forbids both. If only the product is eaten (late grapes), the vow forbids only the product. חכמים follow this rule; the תנא קמא always permits the product.
steps.confusionAlert: In the second case the result flips. The fruit he named is permitted, and the product he did not name is forbidden, because that is what he meant.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows a key rule of נדרים: we read a vow by the person's real intention and normal speech, not only by the literal word he said.

phrases.english: Anything that is not normally eaten as it is,
but what comes out of it is normally eaten,
if he vows off it,
he is forbidden only in what comes out of it,
because this person meant nothing
except what comes out of it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues and completes the ברייתא begun in the previous step
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: When only the product is normally eaten, a vow on the fruit forbids only the product. חכמים hold this distinction; the תנא קמא does not.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: חכמים differ from the תנא קמא by following רבי שמעון בן אלעזר: a vow is read by normal eating habits and the person's intent.

steps.title: New משנה: wine, oil, and honey vows do not include the less common kinds
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that a נדר on wine allows apple wine, a נדר on oil allows sesame oil, and a נדר on honey allows date honey.
steps.simpleTranslation: Someone who vows off wine may still drink apple wine. Someone who vows off oil may still use sesame oil. Someone who vows off honey may still eat date honey.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It lists cases where a person's נדר on a general food word does not cover a less common version of that food.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When people simply say 'wine,' they mean grape wine. When they say 'oil,' they mean olive oil, and 'honey' means bee honey. The other kinds always need an extra word (apple, sesame, date), so a plain נדר does not reach them.

keyTerms.meaning: Short for מַתְנִיתִין: 'our משנה.' It marks the start of a new משנה.
One who makes a נדר (a vow forbidding something to himself)
Permitted
Apple wine (cider)
Sesame oil
Date honey

phrases.english: MISHNA:
One who vows off wine
is permitted to drink apple wine
One who vows off oil
is permitted to use sesame oil
One who vows off honey
is permitted to eat date honey

steps.triggerLanguage: הַנּוֹדֵר מִן הַיַּיִן מוּתָּר בְּיֵין תַּפּוּחִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new משנה. It moves from vows on fruits and their products to vows on general food words.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A נדר on a general food word forbids only its standard kind. Kinds that need an extra describing word (apple wine, sesame oil, date honey) remain permitted.

steps.title: משנה continues: vinegar, leeks, and vegetables, and the reason behind the rule
steps.stepSummary: The משנה continues with three more cases and then gives the reason: these kinds have a name with an added describing word.
steps.simpleTranslation: Someone who vows off vinegar may still use vinegar made from late grapes. Someone who vows off leeks may still eat קפלוטות. Someone who vows off vegetables may still eat wild field vegetables, because that kind is called by a name with an extra word attached.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה finishes its list. At the end it states the reason for all these cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The closing phrase שֶׁהוּא שֵׁם לְוַוי explains the whole list. Any kind that people call by the basic name plus an extra word is not included when someone uses just the basic name in a נדר.

keyTerms.meaning: Late-ripening grapes, picked in the winter season
Leeks
A type of leek with its own name
Wild field vegetables
A name with an added describing word, not the plain name

steps.whatToRemember: A plain word in a נדר covers only what people normally mean by that plain word. Anything that needs an extra describing word is left out.

phrases.english: One who vows off vinegar
is permitted to use vinegar of late grapes
One who vows off leeks
is permitted to eat kaflutot
phrases.notes: קפלוטות are a kind of leek, but people call them by their own name.

phrases.english: One who vows off vegetables
is permitted to eat field vegetables
because it is a name with an added word
phrases.notes: Literally 'an accompanying name.' People don't just say 'vegetables'; they say 'field vegetables.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same list from the משנה and adds the reason that explains every case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Late-grape vinegar, kaflutot, and field vegetables are permitted after a plain נדר, because each is a שֵׁם לְוַוי.

steps.title: ברייתא: what 'oil' means depends on the place
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that a נדר on oil means olive oil in ארץ ישראל and sesame oil in בבל. Where both are used, both are forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: someone who vows off oil in ארץ ישראל may use sesame oil but not olive oil. In בבל, he may not use sesame oil but may use olive oil. In a place where people use both kinds, both are forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that adds a detail to the משנה's oil case. The meaning of 'oil' depends on where the person lives.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה said sesame oil is permitted, but that was true only in ארץ ישראל, where 'oil' means olive oil. In בבל, sesame oil was the common oil, so the result flips. Where both oils are common, the plain word 'oil' covers both.

keyTerms.meaning: Short for גְּמָרָא. It marks the start of the גמרא's discussion.
'It was taught.' This introduces a ברייתא.
Olive oil
Forbidden
People use or supply themselves with

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the meaning of a נדר follows how people actually speak in that place. The same words can forbid different things in different countries.

phrases.english: GEMARA:
It was taught in a baraita:
One who vows off oil
in Eretz Yisrael
is permitted to use sesame oil
and is forbidden to use olive oil
And in Babylonia
he is forbidden to use sesame oil
phrases.notes: In בבל, sesame oil was the everyday oil, so plain 'oil' meant sesame oil there.

phrases.english: and is permitted to use olive oil
A place where people use both this and that
he is forbidden to use both this and that

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא הַנּוֹדֵר מִן הַשֶּׁמֶן בְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the משנה's oil case and shows that its ruling depends on local usage.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Oil in a נדר means the locally standard oil. Where two oils are both in use, both are forbidden.

steps.title: Isn't the last ruling obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא's final ruling, that both oils are forbidden where both are used, as too obvious to need saying.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions why the ברייתא needed to say that both oils are forbidden in a place where both are used. That seems obvious.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If both oils are called 'oil' in that place, the plain word clearly covers both. So the line seems to teach nothing new, and the גמרא pushes back on it.

keyTerms.meaning: 'It is obvious!' A challenge claiming that a statement is unnecessary.

phrases.english: That's obvious!
phrases.notes: This is aimed at the last line of the ברייתא, about a place where people use both oils.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the final clause of the ברייתא in step 8.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's ruling that both oils are forbidden where both are used
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If both oils are commonly called 'oil' there, it is self-evident that both are included, so the clause seems unnecessary.

steps.title: Needed even where most people use one kind: a doubt about something forbidden is treated strictly
steps.stepSummary: The ruling is needed for a place where most people use one kind of oil. We do not follow the majority, because ספק איסורא לחומרא.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed for a place where most people use one kind. You might have thought: let me follow the majority. So the ברייתא teaches that when there is a doubt about something forbidden, we are strict.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the 'obvious' challenge. It explains that the ruling covers a less obvious case, where only most people use one kind.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If most people use olive oil and only a minority use sesame oil, we might think 'oil' means only the majority's oil. The ברייתא teaches that sesame oil is still forbidden. Since the word might include it, this is a doubt about something forbidden, and such a doubt is treated strictly.

keyTerms.meaning: 'It is not needed except for...' This introduces the less obvious case a ruling is meant for.
The majority
'You might have said.' This introduces a mistaken first thought.
'It teaches us.'
A doubt about something forbidden is treated strictly

steps.whatToRemember: Where both oils are used, even if one is used by only a minority, a נדר on 'oil' forbids both, because ספק איסורא לחומרא.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't assume 'follow the majority' always decides. Here the question is what the word 'oil' might include. Since it may include the minority's oil, the doubt makes that oil forbidden too.

phrases.english: No, it is needed
where most people use one kind
You might have said:
Let me follow the majority
So it teaches us
a doubt about something forbidden is treated strictly

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא צְרִיכָא דְּרוּבָּא מִן חַד מִסְתַּפְּקִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the פשיטא challenge of step 9 by narrowing the ברייתא to a less obvious case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case (לא צריכא): the ruling applies even where one kind is used by the majority
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Follow the majority's usage, so only the majority's oil would be forbidden
steps.terutzMaskana: Both oils are forbidden, because the word may include the minority's oil and ספק איסורא לחומרא

steps.title: A vow on vegetables depends on the year
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues. In the six regular years, a נדר on 'vegetables' forbids garden vegetables and allows field vegetables. In שביעית it is the other way around.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone vows off 'vegetables' during the six regular years, garden vegetables are forbidden to him and field vegetables are allowed. If he makes the vow during שביעית, field vegetables are forbidden and garden vegetables are allowed.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא from step 8 keeps going and adds a new case. It is a נדר on vegetables, and the answer changes depending on which year of the seven-year cycle it is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This works like the oil case: the words of a נדר mean what people usually mean by them in that time and place. In regular years, people mostly eat vegetables grown in gardens. In שביעית the land may not be worked, so people mostly eat vegetables that grow on their own in the field. So the same word, 'vegetables,' points to a different kind.

keyTerms.meaning: Vegetables
The years of the seven-year cycle
The seventh year of the cycle (שמיטה), when the land may not be worked
Garden vegetables, which are planted and tended
Field vegetables, which grow wild

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think field vegetables are always the 'lesser' kind that is left out. Which kind the נדר covers flips in שביעית, because what people normally eat flips.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the meaning of a נדר can change with time, not only with place, as in the oil case.

phrases.english: One who vows off vegetables,
in the other years of the seven-year cycle,
is forbidden to eat garden vegetables,
and is allowed to eat field vegetables.
But in the seventh year,
he is forbidden to eat field vegetables,
and is allowed to eat garden vegetables.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַנּוֹדֵר מִן הַיָּרָק, בִּשְׁאָר שְׁנֵי שָׁבוּעַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the ברייתא of step 8, after the challenge and answer in steps 9 and 10, and adds a second case built on the same idea.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A נדר on vegetables covers whatever vegetables are commonly eaten that year: garden vegetables in regular years, field vegetables in שביעית.

steps.title: Opening a statement of רבי אבהו
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins a statement that רבי אבהו says in the name of רבי חנינא בן גמליאל. The words of the statement come next.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבהו said in the name of רבי חנינא בן גמליאל:
steps.whatsHappening: This line only sets up the next move. The גמרא tells us who is about to speak, and the words of his statement come right after this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing is ruled yet. The line tells us that a later אמורא, רבי אבהו, is passing on a teaching from the earlier sage רבי חנינא בן גמליאל. It most likely relates to the vegetables case just taught.

keyTerms.meaning: He said, the usual way a statement is introduced
In the name of, passing on someone else's teaching
An אמורא of ארץ ישראל

phrases.english: Rabbi Abbahu said
in the name of Rabbi Ḥanina ben Gamliel:

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי חֲנִינָא בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Introduces a teaching that will most likely comment on the vegetables case from step 11.
